MODEL DESIGN

Make the assumptions
part of the conversation.

Educational, fictional acquisition model. No live market data or investment recommendations.

How the economics work

Entry enterprise value = $24m EBITDA × entry multiple. Debt = $24m × leverage; sponsor equity funds the remaining EV plus 2% transaction fees. A debt-free, cash-free acquisition is assumed.

Each year's revenue = prior revenue × (1 + organic growth) × retention × (1 + pricing) + $100m × cross-sell rate × ramp. Growth is modeled before retention and pricing; cross-sell is an annual recurring addition, not cumulative bookings. Ramp is ⅓, ⅔, then 100%.

EBITDA = revenue × margin + ramped synergies. Interest uses opening debt. Tax is 25% of positive EBITDA less 3% revenue D&A and interest; capex is 4% revenue and incremental working capital is 10% of revenue change. Integration cost is split over years 1–2.

Positive free cash flow repays debt, then accumulates cash. Deficits consume cash and can produce a flagged funding gap; no additional financing is assumed. Exit equity = max(0, exit EBITDA × multiple − debt + cash). IRR assumes an initial equity outflow and a single year-five inflow. No interim distributions, interest deduction caps, tax loss carryforwards, purchase accounting, or financing fees.

Simulation and limitations

Monte Carlo uses a seeded linear congruential generator and centered sums of three uniform draws. Growth shocks span ±9 percentage points, exit shocks ±3×, retention shocks ±6 points, then clamp to input bounds. These are illustrative distributions, not calibrated forecasts. Independent variables omit correlations. The model applies no probability of default or recovery waterfall.

Questions to stress-test the thesis

How much of the return comes from earnings growth, multiple change, and debt paydown? Which synergies require the most organizational change? Could a pricing increase damage retention? What evidence would justify the assumed cross-sell rate?
